segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was going out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, look—what stones and what buildings!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus began to say to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Watch out that no one leads you astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will lead many astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. It must happen, but the end is not yet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom; there will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These things are the beginning of the birth pains.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, watch out for yourselves. They will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the good news must first be proclaimed to all the nations.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when they lead you away to hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what you will say, but say whatever is given to you in that hour, for it is not you who are speaking but the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he should not be

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (let the reader understand),

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: then those in Judea must flee to the mountains,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: the one on the housetop must not come down or go inside to take anything out of his house,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the one in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Pray that it may not happen in winter.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For those days will be an affliction such as has not happened from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will happen.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if the Lord had not cut the days short, no flesh would be saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones, whom he chose, he has cut the days short.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Look, there!’ do not believe it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the chosen ones.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, watch out. I have told you everything beforehand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But in those days, after that affliction, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then he will send out the angels and gather the chosen ones from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Learn the parable from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So also you, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, right at the door.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But about that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but only the Father.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Watch out, stay alert, for you do not know when the time is.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like a man away on a journey, who has left his house and given his slaves authority, to each his work, and has commanded the doorkeeper to stay awake.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house is coming, whether in the evening or at midnight or at cockcrow or at dawn—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that he does not come suddenly and find you sleeping.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And what I say to you I say to everyone: Stay awake.”

notes.note: The Greek is simply “I am,” with no complement. In context it most naturally means “I am the one,” that is, the Messiah, which is how Matthew’s parallel spells it out. Some scholars also hear an echo of the divine self-declaration “I am” from the Greek Old Testament; the wording allows this, but it cannot be proved.

The Greek word here is the same one that in the plural is often translated “Gentiles,” the non-Jewish peoples. In this verse and in “all the nations” in verse 10 it means peoples as such, so “nation” is used. The reader should know that one Greek word lies behind both English words across the New Testament.

The word means the pains of a woman in labor. The prophets used labor as an image for the anguish that comes before God’s deliverance, and later Jewish writers spoke in similar terms of the suffering that would precede the age to come. The image implies that the pain leads to something and is not the end itself.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody. Mark uses the same word for what Judas, the chief priests, and Pilate do to Jesus, so one rendering is kept throughout to let the reader see that the disciples’ fate mirrors their teacher’s. Many versions vary it with “deliver up,” “arrest,” or “betray” (as in verse 12).

The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book, so the plainer rendering is used. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The phrase comes from the book of Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it refers to a detestable object set up in the temple that leaves it defiled and deserted; Jewish readers connected it with the pagan altar erected by Antiochus IV in 167 BC. “Abomination” in the Greek Old Testament regularly means something idolatrous. What event Jesus’ saying points to is disputed: proposals include events of the Jewish war of AD 66–70 and a still-future figure.

notes.phrase: standing where he should not be
notes.note: The noun “abomination” is neuter in Greek, but the participle “standing” is masculine, which suggests that Mark thinks of a person. Most English versions smooth this over with “it”; the masculine is kept here because the grammatical mismatch appears deliberate. It is possible, though less likely, that the masculine is merely loose grammar.

This is usually taken as an aside by Mark to the person reading the Gospel aloud to a congregation, signaling that the cryptic phrase needs careful interpretation; it is labeled as the narrator’s words on that view. It could instead be part of Jesus’ speech, referring to the reader of Daniel. The Greek does not settle the question.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for oppressive hardship, not a technical name. “Tribulation” is now widely heard as the title of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. “Affliction” is itself a long-standing rendering of the word and is used for it throughout this translation. The sentence echoes Daniel 12:1.

“All flesh” is a Hebrew idiom for all living people. “Saved” here refers in the first instance to physical survival: no one would come through alive. Many modern versions paraphrase as “no one would survive.”

notes.phrase: the chosen ones, whom he chose
notes.note: The noun and the verb share a root in Greek, and the repetition is deliberate. “The elect” hides that link and has become a term of later theological debate; “chosen ones” is what the word plainly means and echoes the Old Testament’s language for Israel as God’s chosen people. Many versions keep “the elect.”

The Greek word, traditionally rendered “Christ,” translates the Hebrew “Messiah,” the anointed king Israel expected. Here it is a title under discussion, not a name, so “Messiah” is used; “false messiahs” in verse 22 is a compound of the same word. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

notes.traditional: the powers that are in heaven
notes.note: Verses 24–25 draw on prophetic imagery, especially Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4, where the darkening of sun, moon, and stars accompanies God’s judgment on nations. “The powers in the heavens” are the heavenly bodies, perhaps thought of as the spiritual forces associated with them. Interpreters differ on whether the language describes a literal cosmic collapse or is the prophets’ customary way of depicting world-shaking historical events. The Greek plural “heavens” is kept.

notes.phrase: the Son of Man coming in clouds
notes.traditional: the Son of man coming in the clouds
notes.note: The wording comes from Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion. Most interpreters take the saying here to refer to Jesus’ return; a minority read it, with Daniel, as a coming to God for vindication and enthronement.

The Greek verb has no expressed subject and can mean “he is near” (the Son of Man) or “it is near” (the end, or the event just described). “He” is chosen because of the image of someone at the door and the returning master in verses 34–36. Translations are divided.

In ordinary usage the word means the people alive at one time, and elsewhere in Mark “this generation” refers to Jesus’ contemporaries. How this fits with what follows is one of the most debated questions in the chapter: some take “all these things” to be the events leading up to the temple’s destruction in AD 70, others take the saying to cover the end itself. Proposals that the word means “race” or “kind of people” have little support in usage of the period.

Many manuscripts read “stay alert and pray,” and older English versions follow them. The words “and pray” are absent from a few important early witnesses and may have been added under the influence of Mark 14:38. The edition translated here omits them.

The Greek word means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. “Servants” softens the picture; the parable assumes a household in which the absent owner’s slaves run his affairs and answer to him on his return. A number of recent translations also use “slaves.”

notes.phrase: in the evening or at midnight or at cockcrow or at dawn
notes.traditional: at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning
notes.note: These are the popular names of the four watches into which the Roman reckoning divided the night, each about three hours long, from sunset to sunrise. The master may return in any of them.
